title: Physical Science: Physics
description: Explain motion, interactions, energy, waves, electricity, and modern physical evidence.

lessons.title: Scalars, vectors and uncertainty
lessons.reading: Scalars have magnitude, while vectors include direction. Displacement differs from path length. Represent vector components consistently and attach units to quantities. Measurements and models have uncertainty; numerical precision should match the evidence.
lessons.worked: Traveling 3 m east then 3 m west gives 6 m distance but zero displacement.

application.explanation: Velocity specifies both speed and direction, unlike the listed scalars.

vocab.definition: A quantity with magnitude and direction.
The vector change in position.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Velocity specifies both speed and direction, unlike the listed scalars.

lessons.title: Position and velocity graphs
lessons.reading: Slope on a position-time graph is velocity. Slope on a velocity-time graph is acceleration, and signed area gives displacement. Interpret axes before reasoning from a shape: a flat line means different things on different graphs.
lessons.worked: A position increase of 12 m over 3 s gives average velocity 4 m/s.

application.prompt: A horizontal velocity-time line at +5 m/s means…
application.explanation: The velocity is unchanged at +5; the object keeps changing position.

vocab.definition: Rate of change of position.
Rate of change of velocity.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: The velocity is unchanged at +5; the object keeps changing position.

units.title: Motion in one and two dimensions

lessons.title: Constant acceleration and free fall
lessons.reading: Constant-acceleration equations connect displacement, time, velocity, and acceleration. Near Earth's surface, ideal free fall has downward acceleration about 9.8 m/s² regardless of mass when air resistance is negligible. Choose a sign convention before substituting.
lessons.worked: Starting from rest at 2 m/s², velocity after 3 s is 6 m/s.

application.prompt: An object starts from rest with acceleration 4 m/s² for 2 s. Its final velocity is…

vocab.definition: Motion under gravity alone.
Velocity at the chosen starting time.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.

lessons.title: Projectile and circular motion
lessons.reading: In ideal projectile motion, horizontal and vertical components evolve independently. Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity because direction changes. Its acceleration points toward the circle's center and requires a net inward force.
lessons.worked: A horizontally launched projectile accelerates vertically but not horizontally in the ideal model.

application.prompt: Uniform circular motion has acceleration directed…
application.explanation: Velocity changes direction, requiring centripetal acceleration inward.

vocab.definition: An object moving under gravity after launch, neglecting other forces in the ideal model.
Inward acceleration associated with circular motion.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Velocity changes direction, requiring centripetal acceleration inward.

lessons.title: Newton's laws and force diagrams
lessons.reading: A force diagram shows forces on one chosen object, not forces it exerts on others. Net force determines acceleration through Fnet = ma. Balanced forces mean zero acceleration, not necessarily zero velocity. Action-reaction forces act on different objects.
lessons.worked: An object moving at constant velocity can have balanced forces.

application.prompt: A 2 kg object has net force 10 N. Its acceleration is…

vocab.definition: The vector sum of forces acting on an object.
Resistance to a change in velocity associated with mass.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.

lessons.title: Friction and gravitation
lessons.reading: Friction depends on surfaces and normal force in common models. Gravitational force follows an inverse-square relationship between point masses or suitable spherical masses. A field describes the force a test object would experience per relevant property.
lessons.worked: Doubling separation reduces ideal gravitational force to one quarter.

application.prompt: Two masses keep the same values but their separation doubles. Gravitational force becomes…

vocab.definition: Gravitational force per unit mass.
A contact force perpendicular to a surface.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.

lessons.title: Impulse and momentum
lessons.reading: Momentum is mass times velocity. Impulse is force integrated over time and equals momentum change. Increasing collision duration can reduce average force for the same momentum change, which helps explain safety designs.
lessons.worked: A helmet can reduce average impact force by lengthening stopping time.

application.prompt: For the same momentum change, doubling stopping time makes average force…
application.explanation: Average force equals momentum change divided by elapsed time.

vocab.definition: The vector quantity mass times velocity.
The change in momentum produced by force over time.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Average force equals momentum change divided by elapsed time.

lessons.title: Conservation in interactions
lessons.reading: A system's total momentum is conserved when external impulse is negligible. Kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision, but not every collision is elastic. Momentum transfer and energy transformation must be analyzed separately.
lessons.worked: Two carts sticking together conserve total momentum in an isolated collision but transform kinetic energy.

application.prompt: Which quantity is conserved in an isolated inelastic collision?
application.explanation: Internal interactions transfer momentum between objects without changing the system total.

vocab.definition: A system with negligible relevant external interactions.
A collision in which total kinetic energy is not conserved.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Internal interactions transfer momentum between objects without changing the system total.

lessons.title: Work and mechanical energy
lessons.reading: Work transfers energy through a force acting along displacement. Kinetic energy is mv²/2 and gravitational potential energy near Earth changes by mgΔh. Energy conservation accounts for all forms, including thermal energy when friction acts.
lessons.worked: Doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy if mass stays constant.

application.prompt: A fixed-mass object's speed triples. Its kinetic energy becomes…
application.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so the factor is 3².

vocab.definition: Energy transfer by force acting through displacement.
The rate of energy transfer.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared, so the factor is 3².

lessons.title: Thermal transfer and efficiency
lessons.reading: Heating can change temperature or phase. Thermal energy transfers from hotter to colder systems without additional intervention. Efficiency compares useful output with input; total energy remains conserved even when useful output is smaller. Devices often transfer some energy as dispersed heat.
lessons.worked: A device giving 60 J useful output for 100 J input is 60% efficient.

application.prompt: A device has 200 J input and 50 J useful output. Efficiency is…

vocab.definition: Useful output energy divided by input energy.
Energy per unit mass per degree of temperature increase.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.

lessons.title: Wave quantities and superposition
lessons.reading: Waves transfer energy and information without net transport of the medium across the whole path. Speed equals frequency times wavelength. Amplitude relates to disturbance size. Superposition combines disturbances where waves overlap, producing interference patterns.
lessons.worked: A wave with frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 2 m travels at 10 m/s.

application.prompt: For constant wave speed, increasing frequency decreases…
options: The number of cycles per second
application.explanation: v = fλ, so λ decreases when f rises at fixed v.

vocab.definition: Cycles per unit time.
Distance between corresponding points of successive cycles.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: v = fλ, so λ decreases when f rises at fixed v.

lessons.title: Reflection, refraction and communication
lessons.reading: Reflection returns waves from a boundary; refraction changes direction when wave speed changes across media at suitable incidence. Diffraction spreads waves around openings. Doppler shifts arise from relative source-observer motion. Digital encoding supports reliable information transfer but has sampling limits.
lessons.worked: Ultrasound echoes can locate boundaries; Doppler shifts can estimate flow speed.

application.prompt: When light enters another medium and changes speed and direction, the effect is…
application.explanation: Refraction arises from changing propagation speed at a boundary, except direction need not change at normal incidence.

vocab.definition: A wave's change of propagation direction associated with a speed change.
A frequency shift due to relative motion.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Refraction arises from changing propagation speed at a boundary, except direction need not change at normal incidence.

lessons.title: Charge, fields and potential
lessons.reading: Electric charge is conserved. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. An electric field gives force per unit positive test charge; potential difference is energy transferred per charge. Field diagrams represent direction and relative strength, not literal threads.
lessons.worked: A positive test charge accelerates in the electric-field direction if other forces are negligible.

application.prompt: Electric field direction is defined by force on a…
application.explanation: The conventional direction is the force on a positive test charge.

vocab.definition: Electric force per unit positive test charge.
Energy change per unit charge.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: The conventional direction is the force on a positive test charge.

lessons.title: Current, resistance and circuits
lessons.reading: Current is charge flow rate. For an ohmic component, V = IR. Series elements share current; parallel branches share potential difference. Conserve charge at junctions and track energy transfers around loops. Power can be calculated as VI.
lessons.worked: A 6 V source across a 3 Ω ohmic resistor produces 2 A.

application.prompt: Two resistors are connected in parallel. What is the same across both?
application.explanation: Parallel branches connect the same pair of circuit nodes, giving the same voltage.

vocab.definition: Charge passing a point per unit time.
The ratio of potential difference to current for a specified operating condition.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Parallel branches connect the same pair of circuit nodes, giving the same voltage.

lessons.title: Magnetic interactions and induction
lessons.reading: Moving charges and currents produce magnetic effects. Magnetic forces can change charged-particle direction without doing work through that force alone. Changing magnetic flux can induce an electromotive force. Generators and motors exchange mechanical and electrical energy through interactions.
lessons.worked: Moving a magnet relative to a coil can induce a changing electrical response.

options: Charge into mass in every case
application.explanation: Mechanical work drives electromagnetic induction to transfer energy electrically.

vocab.definition: Generation of an electrical effect by changing magnetic flux.
A representation of magnetic interactions.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Mechanical work drives electromagnetic induction to transfer energy electrically.

lessons.title: Light, photons and nuclear evidence
lessons.reading: Light displays wave phenomena and quantized interactions. Photon energy is hf. Spectra indicate discrete atomic energy changes; the photoelectric effect supports quantized energy transfer. Nuclear reactions involve different energy scales and particle changes than chemical reactions.
lessons.worked: Increasing photon frequency increases its energy without requiring an increased photon count.

options: The one with longer wavelength always
application.explanation: E = hf with constant positive h, so energy increases with frequency.

vocab.definition: A quantum of electromagnetic radiation.
Emission of electrons from material through absorption of sufficiently energetic radiation.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: E = hf with constant positive h, so energy increases with frequency.

lessons.title: Test models and analyze uncertainty
lessons.reading: A model predicts relationships under stated assumptions. Compare predictions with data, residuals, and uncertainty rather than expecting exact agreement. Control variables and repeat measurements. A mismatch can reveal measurement limits, missing forces, or an unsuitable approximation.
lessons.worked: A no-air-resistance model may fail for a light object falling through air.

application.prompt: Which is the best response to repeated disagreement with a prediction?
application.explanation: Evidence should guide revision of assumptions, procedures, or the model.

vocab.definition: The chosen limit separating a system from its surroundings.
A limit on the precision or confidence of a result.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: Evidence should guide revision of assumptions, procedures, or the model.

lessons.title: Design for performance and trade-offs
lessons.reading: Engineering uses physics to meet criteria within constraints. Compare alternative designs with measurable tests and justify revisions. Safety, energy use, cost, and material availability can conflict. A successful design is supported by evidence rather than attractive presentation alone.
lessons.worked: Compare helmet designs using peak force, stopping duration, mass, and repeated-test consistency.

application.prompt: Which is a measurable performance criterion for a helmet?
application.explanation: A force limit measures desired performance, whereas budget and deadline are constraints.

vocab.definition: A target used to judge a solution.
A restriction limiting a design.

lessons.practice: Explain your choice using the relationship or evidence in this lesson.
lessons.reflection: A force limit measures desired performance, whereas budget and deadline are constraints.
